source: Ginns (2006) Integrating information: meta-analysis of spatial and temporal contiguity
finding: Integrated formats beat separated formats on learning. Seen only through citing papers, not opened.
numbers: Weighted mean d = 0.85, 95% CI 0.68-1.02; 50 studies, 2,375 novice learners (as cited by He and Loewen 2024). A German review of Schroeder and Cenkci quotes g = 0.72 on 37 effects for Ginns, and de Koning 2020 quotes a median d = 0.72, so reports differ.
limits: Mostly novices, short lab studies. Sources disagree on which Ginns number is which; check the original before citing.
agent_relevance: Prior for how large a gain from merging related text could be for a reader with limited working memory. Do not assume it transfers to a model.

source: Schroeder and Cenkci (2018) Spatial contiguity and spatial split-attention effects: meta-analysis (via German Clearing House review)
finding: Update of Ginns with 21 new comparisons. Integrated beats separated, but by less than in Ginns. I read a German summary of the paper, not the paper.
numbers: Overall g = 0.63 on 58 effects (Ginns in the same summary: g = 0.72 on 37 effects). Worksheets g = 0.80; 2-D figures g = 0.71; when figure and text complement each other g = 0.72. Subject: biology/geography medium, technology medium, maths/physics small. Grades 6-8 small, grades 9-12 large. Europe small effect. Intervention length, retention vs transfer, and test format were not significant moderators.
limits: Secondary summary only. Reviewer says the smaller effect is probably due to more varied modern media.
agent_relevance: Effect has shrunk as studies diversified. Expect a modest, material-dependent gain from integrating, not a universal one.

source: Wang et al. (2016) Text-picture integration in multimedia learning: meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity effect (Chinese journal)
finding: Third meta-analysis: contiguity helps retention and transfer and lowers rated load. Only a search snippet was seen.
numbers: 53 studies. Retention d = 0.48, transfer d = 0.39, subjective cognitive load d = -0.24. Moderators for transfer: element interactivity, pacing, learning duration.
limits: Abstract level only. Smaller than Ginns.
agent_relevance: A more conservative estimate; rated load falls less than learning rises.

source: Cammeraat, Rop and de Koning (2020) The influence of spatial distance and signaling on the split-attention effect
finding: Failed replication. Distance and signaling did nothing in Exp 1, and Exp 2 found no split-attention effect at all on retention, transfer or effort.
numbers: Exp 1: 2x2 (distance x signaling), error df 103 so about 107 people; no effect of distance or signaling on effort or transfer; Bayes factors 3 to 23 in favour of no effect (distance BF null 4.72, interaction BF null 22.94). Exp 2: online replication of Johnson and Mayer (2012), car braking system; error df 137 so about 140 people; condition effect F(2,137)=1.91 p=.153, BF null 5.11.
quote: raise doubts about how robust the split-attention effect is
limits: Online (Mechanical Turk) sample, one topic, short study. Authors say the effect may be very small or absent with these materials.
agent_relevance: Even the best-known effect is not guaranteed. Test any prompt-format change against a control before keeping it (guardrail G7).

source: Pouw, Rop, de Koning, Tabbers and Paas (2019) The cognitive basis for the split-attention effect, JEP General
finding: Three experiments tested whether distance itself causes the effect. Distance changed process measures but not learning. Abstract only (search results and Cammeraat's description).
numbers: Exp 1 (two pictures): more distance hurt a visual working-memory secondary task, not integration speed. Exp 2 (text+picture, preregistered): more distance slowed integration, not the secondary task. Exp 3 (nervous-system materials; integrated vs small gap vs large gap): no split-attention effect on learning or effort.
limits: Not opened beyond abstract. Signaling was in both separated conditions in Exp 3, a possible explanation per Cammeraat.
agent_relevance: Supports a rival view: separation alone is not the harm; the harm is the integration work, which a cue can remove.

source: Beege, Wirzberger, Nebel, Schneider, Schmidt and Rey (2019) Spatial continuity effect vs spatial contiguity failure
finding: Two experiments on how close text should be to the picture. Separated did not lose to integrated in Exp 1. Best transfer came at medium proximity, an inverted U.
numbers: Exp 1 N=98: separated vs integrated retention t=0.66 p=.51; transfer t=1.47 p=.15; quadratic contrast for transfer t=2.19 p=.03. Exp 2 N=85: retention r=.22, transfer r=.27.
limits: Prior knowledge and spatial ability were significant covariates. Authors note many studies do not describe the integrated condition.
agent_relevance: Closer is not always better. Test placement levels, not just yes/no.

source: Beege et al. (2019) review of failed and partial replications
finding: Names studies that failed or partly failed: Schmidt-Weigand et al. (2010) could not replicate; Florax and Ploetzner (2010) found no significant difference between separated and labeled presentation; Pouw et al. (2019) Exp 3 no effect.
numbers: No pooled numbers. At least 3 named non-replications or partial replications.
limits: Reported second-hand inside Beege et al.
agent_relevance: Single-study evidence is mixed even though pooled effects are positive. Expect some publication-bias inflation.

source: Beege et al. (2019) complexity moderator of the split-attention effect
finding: Effect depends on element interactivity: large with complex material, not significant with simple material.
numbers: d=0.78 for high-complexity material, d=0.28 (p>.05) for low complexity. Beege attributes these to Cohen (1988) citation chain, so check the original.
limits: Second-hand figures.
agent_relevance: Splitting matters only when pieces must be combined; for simple items do not bother reformatting. Links to intrinsic load subfield.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1999) Managing split-attention and redundancy in multimedia instruction, Exp 1 (audio text)
finding: Split attention can be reduced without physical integration. Replacing on-screen text with audio gave the best results for novices.
numbers: 34 first-year trade apprentices, 3 groups (visual text, visual+audio text, audio text). Effectiveness differed: fault-finding F(2,31)=7.74, multiple choice F(2,31)=10.66; audio group best.
limits: Small sample. Duplicate visual+audio text lost its advantage (redundancy). Novices only.
agent_relevance: Audio has no prompt analogue; the lesson is that a second channel can relieve load. Do not assume it helps if content is duplicated.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1999), Exp 2 (colour coding)
finding: Colour-coding diagram parts and matching text lowered effort and raised multiple-choice scores compared with a conventional separate layout.
numbers: 16 trainees, 8 per group. Multiple choice (covarying instruction time) F(1,13)=7.17; effort rating F(1,13)=3.09 marginal; fault-finding F(1,13)=0.78 not significant; effectiveness on multiple choice F(1,13)=7.01.
limits: Tiny sample. One of two outcome measures showed no effect.
agent_relevance: Tagging which text goes with which item (IDs, colours, brackets) is a cheap substitute for physical integration.

source: Kalyuga et al. (1999) redundancy boundary
finding: Presenting the same text both on screen and as audio did not beat audio alone for novices, so a duplicate source adds load.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=34): Audio-text group in the high-effectiveness area; visual text and visual+audio groups lower.
limits: Same small sample.
agent_relevance: Restating the same rule twice in a prompt is not free: drop redundant restatements.

source: de Koning, Rop and Paas (2020) Learning from split-attention materials: teaching physical and mental learning strategies
finding: Telling learners to mentally integrate separated text and picture reduced the split-attention loss to about the level of an integrated layout.
numbers: N=87 learned about an electrical circuit. Recall F(3,87)=5.38 p<.001 partial eta2=.163; comprehension F(3,87)=6.32; causal inference F(3,87)=0.73 ns. Mental strategy vs split no-strategy: recall d=0.77, comprehension d=0.94. Integrated vs split no-strategy: recall d=1.11, comprehension d=0.81 (as the paper reports the split-attention effect). Ginns (2006) median d=0.72 cited for comparison.
limits: One topic, one lab, same group as earlier studies. No effect on causal inference.
agent_relevance: An instruction such as 'link each item to its rule before answering' may match rewriting the layout. Cheap to test.

source: de Koning et al. (2020) imagination effect comparison
finding: The mental-strategy gain is of the size seen in earlier imagination-effect work.
numbers: Imagination effect sizes cited: d=1.30 (Exp 1), d=0.86 (Exp 2).
limits: Cross-study comparison, not head to head.
agent_relevance: Self-integration cues have a record as a learning strategy.

source: He and Loewen (2024) Presenting L2 Chinese words effectively: adjacent vs horizontal vs vertical format
finding: Split attention applies outside science: putting character, pinyin and meaning adjacent helped, but a vertical layout did not beat horizontal.
numbers: Adjacent format gave 1.23x higher odds of a correct answer than horizontal on recognition and meaning recall. Form recall hit a floor. Preference ratings did not match gains (adjacent was least preferred). 34 s study time per word.
limits: Immediate posttest; low-proficiency learners; lab.
agent_relevance: Users and judges may prefer formats that do not help; measure outcomes, not impressions.

source: Yeung (1997, 1999), Genc and Gulozer (2013), Al-Shehri and Gitsaki (2010) as reported by He and Loewen (2024)
finding: Reversals and nulls: integrated glosses helped low-proficiency readers' comprehension but hurt vocabulary learning, and the pattern reversed for more proficient readers; 5th and 8th graders showed opposite patterns; online reading showed no integrated-vs-separated difference.
numbers: No numbers given in the source.
limits: Second-hand, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Task type and learner level can flip the sign. Do not apply integration blindly.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC)
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to a math problem breaks prompting methods. Mitigations: an explicit 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction, exemplars with distractors, and self-consistency.
numbers: Of base problems the baseline solved, no more than 18% were solved for all distractor types; fewer than 30% consistently solved after distractors. Self-consistency with 20 samples: more than +11 points micro accuracy (+35.5 on 0-CoT); correct answer present in the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems; best macro accuracy only 45%. Instruction and distractor exemplars did not hurt GSM8K dev (59.3 vs 60.3 with instruction) or SVAMP (79.1 vs 77.6). Role-overlap and in-topic irrelevant sentences hurt most; number size mattered little.
quote: Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.
limits: Old models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Problem set built from GSM8K. Newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that irrelevant text in a prompt is a cost. Only the sentence about ignoring irrelevant information changed behaviour; 'Solve grade school math problems' alone did not.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic and GSM-NoOp, ICLR
finding: Adding a plausible but inconsequential clause to a math problem cuts accuracy sharply across models; 8 shots of the same question did not fix it.
numbers: GSM-NoOp: drops up to 65% across models (Phi-3-mini over 65%); o1-preview also fell significantly. NoOp-Symb (8 shots of the same question with the reasoning chain) stayed within one standard deviation of the baseline.
quote: models tend to convert statements to operations without truly understanding their meaning
limits: Math word problems only; per-model numbers are in figures I did not transcribe.
agent_relevance: Plausible but irrelevant facts are the worst kind: models turn them into operations. Remove them rather than ask the model to skip them.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (S2A)
finding: Having the model first rewrite the input to drop irrelevant or opinionated parts, then answer from the rewrite, raises accuracy.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat: factual QA with opinions 62.8% baseline, 80.3% S2A, 82.0% clean-prompt oracle. GSM-IC in-topic distractors 51.7% to 61.3%; random distractors about +12 points, in-topic about +10 (100 problems, 3 seeds).
limits: One model family, small test sets. Costs an extra generation. The model does the cleaning, so it can drop needed text.
agent_relevance: A clean-the-context step is a tested way to drop irrelevant text; have code check that nothing needed was removed.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context length alone hurts LLM performance despite perfect retrieval
finding: Even when retrieval is perfect, longer input lowers accuracy, including when the filler is whitespace or masked.
numbers: 5 models on math, QA, coding: drops of 13.9% to 85% as input grows, within claimed context length. Table 2 (three lengths): Claude-3.7-Sonnet GSM8K -7.0, -8.5, -7.0; Gemini GSM8K -3.8, -5.2, -6.0; open models: Llama VarSum -48%, Mistral GSM8K -30%. Some closed models near flat (GPT-4o GSM8K +7.7, +8.6, +6.2).
limits: Drop depends on model and task; some frontier models were robust on some tasks.
agent_relevance: Length is a cost separate from distraction. Keep prompts short even when everything in them is relevant.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Models use information at the start and end of the context best and the middle worst. Where related items sit changes accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA drops by more than 20% from best to worst position; at 20 and 30 documents the worst case is below closed-book 56.1% (oracle 88.3%). Key-value retrieval: with query-aware contextualization (question before and after the documents) GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) is perfect at 300 pairs; without it the worst case is 45.6%.
limits: 2023 models; newer models reduced the effect.
agent_relevance: Put the question next to the data it needs and key facts at the edges. Query-aware placement is the prompt-side analogue of putting the label next to the referent.

source: Sclar et al. (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (FormatSpread)
finding: Meaning-preserving format changes alter accuracy a lot, so format effects are noisy and one A/B pair proves little.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats for LLaMA-2-13B. GPT-3.5 spread up to 56 points, median 6.4, across 320 formats.
limits: Formats vary separators, casing and spacing, not integration of references.
agent_relevance: Any layout test needs many formats and a reported spread, not one comparison.

source: Interleaved Cognitive Evaluation, arXiv 2509.19517 (Cognitive load limits in LLMs)
finding: Interleaving irrelevant segments among relevant multi-hop steps lowers accuracy in the one model that scored above zero.
numbers: 200 questions, 5 models, 10 replications. Gemini-2.0-Flash: control 0.85, long control 0.82 (p=.45), saturation 80% 0.72, residue 0.78 (p=.12); slope -0.003 per 1% extraneous load (CI -0.004 to -0.002). GPT-4o 0.65 to 0.55 (slope p=.07; 32% of outputs lacked a final answer). Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B and Mistral-7B scored 0.00 in all cells. Gemini hop recall 0.90 to 0.75.
limits: Single-author preprint. Only one non-confounded model. Length-matched filler did not hurt, so irrelevance rather than length drove the drop.
agent_relevance: Distractors interleaved among needed steps cost about 13 points for a strong model; distractors placed before the needed text hurt less (not significant).

source: ToolLoad-Bench, arXiv 2601.20412 (cognitive load framework for tool-use agents)
finding: Benchmark with adjustable intrinsic and extraneous load; reports performance cliffs as load rises. Only the abstract was seen.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Might give agent-level load thresholds; needs full text.

source: Cognitive Overload Attack, arXiv 2410.11272
finding: Claims that raising intrinsic and extraneous load in a prompt breaks model guardrails.
numbers: Attack success up to 99.99% in the search snippet.
limits: Search snippet only. Security setting, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Not evidence for accuracy effects.

source: Cammeraat et al. (2020) listing of fixes for split attention
finding: The introduction lists ways reported to cut the loss: integration, colour coding or signaling, and cues that guide attention; it argues signaling may explain why Pouw et al. (2019) Exp 3 found no effect.
numbers: Examples: Kalyuga et al. 1999 colour coding; De Koning et al. 2009; Johnson and Mayer 2012 eye tracking.
limits: Review sentences, no pooled data.
agent_relevance: Maps to prompt tactics: put labels inline, tag cross-references, do not duplicate content.

source: Synthesis across b01-b26: what holds up, human and LLM
finding: Human pooled effects are positive but shrinking (d 0.85 to g 0.63; d 0.48 retention in Wang) with documented replication failures. LLM studies show clear harm from irrelevant text (up to 65% drop) and gains from removing it (S2A +10 to 12 points). I found no controlled LLM test that moves a referent closer to its rule at equal tokens.
numbers: My own reading of lines above.
limits: Absence of that LLM test is from searches in this session only.
agent_relevance: Highest-value test for our agent: same prompt, referents inline vs listed separately, equal tokens, many formats, with a no-change control.
